aliases: Lao Cong Ju Duo Zai Dancong
processing: Made the way Phoenix dancong usually is: sun-withered, shaken and rested in rounds, then fixed, rolled and dried, with a roast that varies by maker. The very small buds make it hard to pick.
harvest_season: As with most Phoenix dancong, the spring picking is the main and most prized one.
appearance_dry: Shorter, finer strands than most dancong, dark brown with some sheen.
appearance_liquor: Clear golden yellow to light amber, typical of almond-type dancong.
appearance_wet: Small leaves with sharply toothed edges and reddened margins.
taste_profile: Almond in both aroma and flavour, high and clean, with a strong returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: General dancong approach: very hot water and quick pours. Back off the leaf or the time if it turns bitter, and do not leave the leaf sitting in water.

vintage_note: Normally sold by spring harvest of the current year, as is usual for Phoenix dancong, often after a roast and some months of rest. Bottles and bags marked old bush cost more, but tree age is rarely verifiable. Older roasted stock is sold with its year stated.
description:
Ju Duo Zai means roughly 'little saw-bud': the leaf has small, deep, sharp teeth along its edge, like a tiny hacksaw, and the buds are said to be the smallest of any Phoenix dancong. It is the tea most people mean when they talk about the almond aroma type.

Those small buds make it fussy to pick, which is part of why it is rated as a valuable line. The rest of the making follows the usual dancong path of shaking, resting, fixing and drying, and the roast decides whether the almond reads fresh or toasty.

In the cup, look for almond on the nose and on the tongue, then a clean, lasting sweetness in the throat. Brew it like any dancong, hot and fast. Too long a steep gives you bitterness that hides everything good about it.

The two common spellings, 锯朵仔 and 锯剁仔, are the same tea. Almond dancong is not always Ju Duo Zai, so ask for the name and village. Shi Gu Ping sellers also offer it, so compare it with a Wudong lot if you can.
history:
Its age and first selection are not well documented. Chinese tea writing explains the name by the serrated leaf and files it under the almond aroma type, and it appears among the trees named by comparison with animals and objects in a Chinese tea science overview of the Phoenix lines.

One vendor's list of Phoenix trees places a Ju Duo Zai in Hucuo, Wudong Village, at about 1050 m.
